name: Umar Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Umar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I look after the haul roads at the lithium mine. Half the shift I'm on the grader, smoothing out the ruts the big trucks make, and the other half I'm on the water cart, spraying the roads so the dust doesn't choke everyone. It sounds boring, but a bad road wrecks tyres that cost $40,000 each, so it matters. Before shift I check the road reports on the tablet, and I've got an AI app that helps me plan which sections to hit first based on the truck routes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You've set that up yourself? Tell me more about that, and what wears you out.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yeah, nobody asked me to. I photographed the dispatch board for a week and asked the AI to find the pattern in where the trucks were running heavy. My supervisor, Linda, liked it enough to show the manager. What wears me out is the money side. My wife Sara does bookkeeping part-time for a few small businesses, we've got Zain, who's 10, and Nora, who's 6, and the mortgage, and we've got maybe three weeks saved. I'm on the lower pay grade for operators because the road crew is classed lower than truck or shovel crews, which I think is nonsense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a shame, there was some good stuff in there. I'd probably post that people should still use the tools, because they help with small jobs. I'm the guy at crib showing people shortcuts on their phones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be a little disappointed. I've been betting that knowing this stuff would get me noticed and maybe off the lower pay grade. If it fizzles, I'm back to arguing about road crew pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and push to get my road planning idea used across the whole site, with a pay bump for it. I'd also keep building the drone side job, flying roof and fence inspections on weekends, which brings in a few hundred a month. That's our savings, basically.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Nothing's wrong, but nothing's moving either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the drone work.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I got my drone licence last year, did it online in three weekends. Now real estate agents and a couple of farmers pay me to fly over properties, maybe $150 a job. It's small, but it's the only money we put away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the people who think AI is all hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they're half right. It's not magic. But it saved me hours on road planning, so it's not nothing either.

S0.say: He'd say it's a shame because some of the tools are good, and he'd keep showing people shortcuts at crib. He'd post that the tools still help with small jobs.
S0.think: He'd be a little disappointed because he's been betting that knowing these tools would get him noticed and off the lower pay grade. If it fizzles he's back to arguing about road crew pay.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools and pushes for his road-planning idea to be used site-wide with a pay rise. Keeps flying weekend drone inspections that bring in a few hundred a month.
S0.feel: Calm but a bit flat, as if nothing's moving.
S0.quote: I'd say they're half right. It's not magic. But it saved me hours on road planning, so it's not nothing either.
S0.fieldNote: He is the only one on his crew building his own tools, and he hoped AI would lift him out of a lower pay grade. His drone side job is the family's only real saving. The hype scenario disappoints him more than it relieves him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the time to get on board, not to fight it. I'd tell the crew to learn the new systems now, while the company's still paying for training. And I'd say the government should help people who can't keep up, because not everyone can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd do well out of this. Grading and water carts are going to be automated, sure, but someone has to plan and watch the automated fleet, and I'm already doing a version of that. The risk is only if the company hires outsiders instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first three months I'd ask Linda to put me forward for the fleet control training. I'd do an online course in mine scheduling at night, maybe $600, and pay for it with drone money. Within a year I'd aim to be in the control room on a higher grade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty good, actually. A bit of nerves, but mostly I'd feel like it's my turn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said not everyone can keep up. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My offsider on the water cart, Joe. He's 55 and he's a lovely bloke, but his phone is a flip phone. I'd try to help him, but I can't make him want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sara think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say go for it, but don't spend the drone money on courses and leave us with nothing. She's the bookkeeper, she watches every dollar. She'd be right.

S1.say: He'd say it's time to get on board and learn new systems while the company still pays for training. He'd add that government should help people who can't keep up.
S1.think: He expects to do well because someone must plan and watch the automated fleet, and he's already doing a version of that. The only risk is the company hiring outsiders.
S1.do: Asks his supervisor within three months to put him forward for fleet control training. Pays for a $600 online mine scheduling course with drone money, aiming for a higher-grade control room role within a year.
S1.feel: Pretty good with some nerves, like it's finally his turn.
S1.quote: She'd say go for it, but don't spend the drone money on courses and leave us with nothing.
S1.fieldNote: In this picture his early habits pay off, and he sounds the most hopeful of anywhere in the interview. His centrist view shows in wanting both individual effort and government help for those left behind. His wife's caution about money balances his eagerness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan fast, and both sides of politics need to stop point-scoring. People need income while things settle, and companies making billions off robot mines should pay their share. I'd be practical about it, not angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried, because the thing I'm good at, being early, doesn't help if the AI does the planning too. And Sara's bookkeeping would be one of the first things to go, it's numbers on a screen. So both our incomes and the drone money all go at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the two years before, I'd try to get into the fleet control room anyway, for the higher pay while it lasts, and squeeze every dollar into savings. I'd look at the jobs that would still need a person to sign off, like safety checks or site inductions, and ask the AI what certificates those need. Once it arrived, I'd take whatever support was offered and keep looking for gaps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, honestly, though I'd hide it. Like driving the grader at night with one headlight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would two years of warning let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grab the higher pay for maybe eighteen months and put a few thousand away. It's not enough to build anything new. It's like being told the road's closing and you've got time to fill up the tank, not to find another road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still trust the AI tools you use every day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still use them, I'm not going to pretend they're useless. But I'd stop telling everyone at crib how great they are. That would feel a bit off.

S2.say: He'd call for a fast, practical plan with less political point-scoring, income support while things settle and robot-mine companies paying their share.
S2.think: Being early doesn't help if AI does the planning too, and his wife's bookkeeping would be among the first jobs to go. Both incomes and the drone money would vanish at once.
S2.do: Gets into the fleet control room for higher pay in the two years before and saves every dollar. Uses AI to find which sign-off roles like safety checks may need a person and what certificates they need, then takes support once it arrives.
S2.feel: Alarmed but hiding it, like driving at night with one headlight.
S2.quote: It's like being told the road's closing and you've got time to fill up the tank, not to find another road.
S2.fieldNote: His advantage of moving early collapses when the warning is short, and he sees all three household incomes exposed at once. He still searches for gaps rather than giving up. He'd quietly stop promoting AI tools to his workmates.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair run-up and people should use it. I'd say the companies and the government should split the cost of retraining. And I'd tell my crew to start now rather than in year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is enough for me to land somewhere, maybe not in mining. I'd be 48. I think I could get into something like site safety or commissioning the robots for a few years, while there's still a need for people to check them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd get into the control room and start a safety certificate at night. By year two I'd have the drone business doing site surveys for the construction firms building the new automated plants. I'd want three months of savings by year three, which would be a first for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but busy. Busy helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't it a risk to put money into a drone business when robots are coming for hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. But the drone is already a robot, I'm just the one flying it. For a few years someone has to own the gear and do the paperwork. I'd keep it small and not borrow for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zain and Nora?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They're little, so not much. I'd just make sure they see me learning things. Zain already asks the AI about dinosaurs every night, so he's ahead of me.

S3.say: He'd say five years is a fair run-up, with companies and government splitting retraining costs. He'd tell his crew to start now rather than in year four.
S3.think: Five years is enough to land somewhere, maybe outside mining. At 48 he could work in site safety or robot commissioning while people still need to check them.
S3.do: Moves to the control room in year one and starts a night safety certificate. Grows the drone business into site surveys for construction firms by year two, without borrowing, and aims for three months of savings by year three.
S3.feel: Uneasy but busy, and the busyness helps.
S3.quote: But the drone is already a robot, I'm just the one flying it.
S3.fieldNote: With five years he builds a layered plan: a control room job, a certificate and a growing side business. He knows the drone work is exposed too and keeps it small and debt-free. His kids are young, so his focus is modelling learning rather than steering them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is good news, and anyone who wastes it only has themselves partly to blame. The rest is on government and companies to make sure towns like ours aren't left behind. I'd be fairly upbeat about it in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is plenty for me to move twice if I need to. My worry is less about me and more about whether there's anything left in this town to move into. I'd be 53, and we might have to go somewhere bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ride the control room for a few years, grow the drone business slowly and save. Around year five I'd look at whether we should move to the coast city where Sara's sister lives, while the kids are still young enough to change schools. I'd keep a list on my phone of which jobs are disappearing and which aren't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, with a small worry about the town. It feels like something I can get ahead of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the town is dying, yes. I'd rather move at 48 by choice than at 53 because I have to. Sara would want to be near her sister anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years versus ten, what's the real difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five, I'm hanging on in the town. With ten, I can choose. That's the difference.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is good news and wasting it is partly on individuals, with the rest on government and companies to protect towns like his. He'd be upbeat in public.
S4.think: Ten years is plenty to move jobs twice, but he worries whether anything will be left in the town to move into. At 53 they might need to go somewhere bigger.
S4.do: Works in the control room for a few years, grows the drone business slowly and saves. Around year five considers moving to the coast city near his wife's sister while the kids can still change schools.
S4.feel: Mostly fine, with a small worry about the town; something he can get ahead of.
S4.quote: I'd rather move at 48 by choice than at 53 because I have to.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, his worry shifts from himself to the town. He'd choose a move early rather than be forced later, which fits his comfort with risk. He keeps a running list of disappearing jobs, the same habit as his road-planning trick.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it's the one where being early doesn't help. All three of our incomes go at once, and we've got three weeks of money. What would help is a temporary income for families while they reskill, and real jobs that come to towns like ours, not just to the cities.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the pay grades. Road crews, water carts, the jobs people call low-skill are the ones that get cut first and paid least. If things change, I'd want those people looked after first, not last.

headlineQuote: Road crews, water carts, the jobs people call low-skill are the ones that get cut first and paid least.
portrait: Umar Haddad is a 43-year-old grader and water cart operator on the haul roads of a lithium mine, married to a part-time bookkeeper, with two young children and about three weeks of savings. He uses AI daily, built his own road planning trick and runs a small drone inspection side job that is the family's only saving. In the steady change picture he expects to move into the fleet control room and sounds hopeful. In the two-year AGI picture, being early stops helping, and all three household incomes are exposed at once, while ten years lets him choose a move rather than be forced.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because being early doesn't help and all three household incomes go at once with three weeks of savings.
whatWouldHelp: A temporary income for families while they reskill, and real jobs brought to towns like his rather than only to the cities.
